claims.text: Adding a few atomic percent silver during synthesis, followed by thermal processing, will produce silver-rich nanoprecipitates in the high-entropy alloy.
The resulting silver-rich nanoprecipitates will be coherent with the alloy matrix.
The silver-rich nanoprecipitates will be dispersed throughout the matrix and preferentially occur at grain boundaries and near sliding surfaces.
Silver-rich nanoprecipitates will act as self-lubricating sites during sliding.
The soft, low-shear character of silver-rich nanoprecipitates will generate a lubricious interfacial layer during sliding.
Silver-rich nanoprecipitates will bear contact stresses while the alloy is sliding.
Coherent nanoprecipitates can distribute shear and relieve stress concentrations.
Relieving stress concentrations and distributing shear will mitigate wear in the silver-doped alloy.
Silver doping will reduce the coefficient of friction relative to the untreated alloy.
Silver doping will reduce the wear rate relative to the untreated alloy.
The coefficient of friction and wear rate may improve by approximately 20–40% relative to the untreated alloy.
The friction and wear benefits will persist from ambient temperature to temperatures potentially approaching 800 °C.
The self-lubricating effect will remain robust if the silver-rich nanoprecipitates remain coherent and resist coarsening and oxidation.
Extreme thermal or oxidizing conditions that destabilize the nanoprecipitates may limit the tribological benefit.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces can facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations that would otherwise promote premature crack initiation.
The untreated comparator is an undoped high-entropy alloy processed with the same thermal treatment as the silver-doped alloy.
Failure to observe statistically significant reductions in both friction coefficient and wear rate, or failure to form coherent silver-rich nanoprecipitates, would falsify the hypothesis.
